name: Bianca Haddad

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I’m with the independent Work Futures Panel. We have no ties to employers, AI companies, unions, parties or government, and we sell nothing. Your answers are confidential. What does a normal day at work look like?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I am 43, with a bachelor’s degree and several years maintaining parts-ordering software for a tech company. I am an experienced developer, not the quickest in our team, but I know which supplier files cause trouble and which warehouse desk to call. Malik cleans at a hospital; we have two school-age children and a mortgage, and last year’s boiler replacement wiped out our savings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d tell my colleagues the parts-ordering system still needs people who know what happens when a supplier changes a code. I use AI now and then to draft a check, but I compare it with the actual order before a release.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I have a bachelor’s degree and years of software work, but this local firm pays below the usual rate. My partner Malik cleans at a hospital, and with two children and less than a month saved, the mortgage worries me before AI does.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d keep maintaining the supplier import that brings new parts lists into our system and ask the warehouse desk about wrong-code complaints. Malik and I would cancel the paid sports stream this month and put 18 toward the grocery account while both wages continue.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d feel anxious about the household budget. A little AI help is pleasant, but a late mortgage payment would not be.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which complaint is hard to forget?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A garage ordered six brake parts under an old supplier code and got the wrong size. I had to trace which list came in that morning before we could fix the invoice.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why is the cushion so thin after years in software?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We paid for a boiler replacement last spring, then school fees and the mortgage kept coming. I would like a month of breathing room before buying any new tools.

say: I tell colleagues **supplier codes** still need people who know the actual order.
I compare occasional **AI checks** with real parts lists before release.
think: I earn **below usual pay** despite a bachelor’s degree and years in software.
I worry our **thin savings** cannot carry the mortgage if either wage slips.
do: **Keep maintaining** supplier imports and ask the warehouse desk about wrong-code orders.
**Cancel sports streaming** and redirect 18 monthly to groceries while both wages continue.
feel: **Anxious** about the mortgage despite minor AI help.
S0.quote: I would like a month of breathing room before buying any new tools.
fieldNote: A **boiler replacement** explains why experienced work has not produced a cushion.
Her modest AI use is checked against **actual parts orders**, not treated as automatic truth.

steps.text: Keep maintaining supplier-list imports and ask warehouse staff about code errors
Cancel sports streaming and reserve 18 monthly for groceries

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d say AI doing buying, checking and coding will reach our parts system very quickly. I would ask our manager to show which people still approve supplier changes and what happens when a wrong part is sent.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I can handle messy supplier files better than a new hire, but the company might make one person supervise several AI feeds. My hours could shrink, and Malik’s hospital cleaning wage would not cover the mortgage alone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d learn a new AI method for spotting duplicate supplier codes on a copy of old lists, with no real customer orders in it. If it catches the known brake-part error, I’d show my manager and ask for the written plan for staffing; if my hours are cut, I’d look for paid purchasing support openings nearby.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d be anxious and watchful. I like a tool that proves itself, but I do not like not knowing who signs the invoice.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What number would you ask the manager for?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: How many imports one person will review after AI takes the first pass. I would also ask whether the same person is responsible when the supplier sends a wrong file.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you spend money on training?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not now. I can test a method using copies of old work. A course fee would come out of the grocery money.

say: I want **named approvers** for supplier changes even when AI does first checks.
I want a **staffing plan** for each person reviewing AI imports.
think: I think one person may supervise **several AI feeds**, cutting my hours.
I know Malik’s **hospital wage** cannot cover our mortgage alone.
do: **Learn AI duplicate checks** on old supplier lists without customer data.
**Request written staffing plans** if the test catches the known parts error.
**Look for purchasing support** if my hours are cut and openings exist.
feel: **Anxious and watchful** about my hours and who signs wrong invoices.
S1.quote: A course fee would come out of the grocery money.
fieldNote: She tests AI against a **known brake-part error** before proposing it at work.
The **grocery budget** rules out paid courses while savings remain below one month.

steps.text: Learn AI duplicate-code checks using copied old supplier lists
Look for paid purchasing-support openings if developer hours are cut

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d tell the warehouse and software teams that full AGI by 2028 could handle most of my ordering code and supplier checks. Robots for hands-on warehouse work may follow around 2031, but my desk job faces the earlier date.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I expect my wage could be cut before we have rebuilt even one month of bills. Malik’s cleaning work might last longer because it is hands-on, but one wage does not cover the mortgage and children.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d ask our manager this month for written notice if supplier-code roles change, and Malik and I would list bills due before the next pay day. If AGI arrives in 2028 and my job ends, I’d call the lender before arrears and apply for paid warehouse-service openings only where posts exist and wages cover our bills.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d be alarmed. A supplier list can be replaced overnight; the mortgage cannot.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What gets paid first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The mortgage, food and Malik’s bus fare to the hospital. We would pause the children’s paid music lessons if my pay stopped, but I would tell them why.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you move for a job?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Only for a written paid offer that covers moving costs and the new housing payment. There are few software jobs nearby, but I would not pull the children out of school for a rumour.

say: I tell both teams **full AGI in 2028** reaches ordering code and checks.
I know **warehouse robots around 2031** arrive later than my desk-work risk.
think: I expect my **developer wage** could shrink before we rebuild savings.
I know Malik’s **hands-on wage** cannot cover our mortgage alone.
do: **Request written notice**, list next bills and pause paid music lessons if my pay stops.
**Call the lender** before arrears if my job ends after 2028.
**Apply for warehouse service** if displaced and openings cover household bills.
feel: **Alarmed** by fast income loss and an unchanged mortgage.
S2.quote: A supplier list can be replaced overnight; the mortgage cannot.
fieldNote: The **2028 thinking-work date** hits her ordering code before warehouse robots arrive.
Her **bill list** identifies Malik’s bus fare alongside the mortgage and food; she would pause the children’s paid music lessons.

steps.text: Pause paid children’s music lessons if developer pay stops
Apply for paid warehouse-service vacancies if displaced after 2028 and pay covers bills

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d say five years before full AGI in 2031 is long enough to sort out who owns a supplier mistake. Robots may reach warehouse handling around 2034, but that is later than the change to my code.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I could learn more about supplier disputes, but AI may take that reasoning too. Five years gives us a chance to rebuild a small cash cushion if both wages hold and the boiler stays quiet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d ask the purchasing manager for one disputed parts order each month to follow from supplier file to customer credit, on paid time if she approves. We would save 80 monthly while both wages hold; if my developer job ends after 2031, I’d apply for paid supplier-support roles only where vacancies remain and pay covers our bills.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d be anxious but able to prepare with actual cases. I will not count an unapproved visit to purchasing as experience.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you write down about a case?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The file that came in, who checked it, and how the customer was credited. I would ask the purchasing manager whether my explanation matches what happened.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if the manager says no?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep my current duties and ask for old cases stripped of customer names. I would not spend our grocery money on a certificate to replace a refused visit.

say: I want a **named owner** for supplier mistakes before AGI changes the code in 2031.
I see **warehouse robots around 2034** as later than my screen-work risk.
think: I could learn **supplier disputes**, though AI may do the same reasoning.
I might rebuild **cash savings** if both wages hold and the boiler stays sound.
do: **Follow one disputed order** monthly only if the purchasing manager approves paid time.
**Apply for supplier support** if displaced after 2031 and vacancies cover bills.
feel: **Anxious but able** to prepare through approved real cases.
S3.quote: I will not count an unapproved visit to purchasing as experience.
fieldNote: Her learning depends on **purchasing approval** and paid time, not a hypothetical transfer.
She wants **case records** and a small buffer before the AGI date.

steps.text: Follow one disputed order monthly only with purchasing approval on paid time
Save 80 monthly while both household wages continue
Apply for paid supplier-support vacancies if displaced after 2031 and pay covers bills

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d say a decade before full AGI in 2036 lets firms clean up supplier records and let staff learn before changing jobs. Robots for warehouse handling may come around 2039, three years after the code changes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We might have more of the mortgage paid by then, but I cannot assume either child will support us. I could build six months of bills if our wages hold; I still do not know which purchasing jobs survive thinking AI.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d keep maintaining the supplier import and start a notebook of each code error I resolve, with customer names removed. We would save 110 monthly while both wages hold; if my developer role ends after 2036, I’d seek paid supplier-service work only where openings remain and wages cover the mortgage and basic bills.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d feel anxious about the mortgage even with ten years to prepare. I could plan without pretending the job is guaranteed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How will the notebook help?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d keep one page per mistake: old code, new code and who approved the correction. If I apply elsewhere, I can show my code-error method without taking our customers’ details.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you make a family plan too?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Malik and I would review the mortgage balance every six months and tell the children what school costs we can afford. We would not promise a course fee before the savings account has grown.

say: I want **clean supplier records** before AGI reaches our code in 2036.
I know **warehouse robots around 2039** come after the thinking-work change.
think: I might build **six months saved** if both wages hold.
I do not know which **purchasing jobs** survive full thinking AI.
do: **Keep maintaining imports** and record solved code errors without customer names.
**Seek paid supplier service** only if displaced after 2036 and openings cover bills.
feel: **Anxious about the mortgage** despite a longer runway.
S4.quote: I can show my code-error method without taking our customers’ details.
fieldNote: Her **error notebook** preserves evidence of method without customer data.
A **six-month goal** depends on both wages; the mortgage and a possible boiler fault remain present concerns for the family.

steps.text: Keep maintaining supplier imports and record anonymized code errors
Save 110 monthly while both wages continue
Seek paid supplier-service vacancies if displaced after 2036 and pay covers bills

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because my ordering code could go before we save a month of bills. Written notice, a paid warehouse-service opening that covers our mortgage, and time to speak with the lender before arrears would help.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn’t ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You did not ask what happens when the boiler breaks again. We can delay a music lesson, but we cannot heat a house with a future job offer.

headlineQuote: We can delay a music lesson, but we cannot heat a house with a future job offer.
portrait: Bianca is a **43-year-old experienced developer** with a bachelor’s degree, lower pay and less than one month saved.
She and Malik cover **two children** and a mortgage, after a boiler repair drained their buffer.
She uses AI **occasionally**, testing it against known supplier mistakes before trusting it.
Her **ordering code** meets thinking AI first; warehouse robots follow about three years later.
The **2028 case** most threatens an already thin household cushion.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** could remove her software wage before the household rebuilds a month of bills.
whatWouldHelp: **Written notice**, a paid bill-covering opening and early lender contact would help protect the mortgage.
